utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. This is Monday, April 21, 2008 I would like to welcome the lawyers, Defence lawyers as well as the accused. Today we will have a conference according to Rule 73 ter, and to this end the Trial Chamber sent an agenda to the different parties. However, before we move into the agenda I have four oral decisions that I must read. I will read these four oral decisions. I will then give the floor to Mr. Scott. I believe he would like to take the floor. So before we actually address the items that are on the agenda. So first and foremost I would like to ask Mr. Registrar to move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second oral decision, decision on the motion for protection measures of Praljak Defence. On March 31, 2008, the Praljak Defence filed, partially confidentially, a motion for protective measures regarding 16 witnesses. However, the Praljak Defence said that it may request changes to be made to these measures, these protective measures, notably when the witness are about to testify. The Prosecution also noted that it reserved itself the right to raise objections if the Praljak Defence was asking for new protective measures for these witnesses. As of now the Trial Chamber believes that granting provisional protection measures would be premature and that consequently for judicial economy it is best to deny the motion. However, the Trial Chamber is asking the Praljak Defence to file a new motion according to the procedure that the Trial Chamber will determine, its guidelines that are to be issued very soon. So this was the second oral decision. Third oral decision. It will be very short. In application of Rule 67(A) of the Rules, the Trial Chamber is giving the deadline provided for by this Rule at April 28, 2008. This is the deadline at which each Defence team will have to fulfil its obligations regarding disclosure to Prosecution regarding all witness statements. You may read Rule 67(A) of the Rules. There is an error in the transcript. My fellow Judge has shown this. On line 22, page 3, it is not Defence time but Defence team, the Defence teams. Fourth oral decision. This is a long decision, and this has to do with Prosecution. Decision on the request for review or, alternatively, for certification of appeal of January 30, 2008. On January 30, 2008, Prosecution filed a motion for review or possibly for a certification of appeal regarding two decisions made by the Trial Chamber. The Defence filed a joint response on February 13, 2008. At first Prosecution requested the review of the decision to admit a -- the transcript of a testimony according to Rule 92 bis (A) decision which was made by the Trial Chamber on January 23, 2008, and called here under the Brix Andersen decision. The Prosecution is asking for the Trial Chamber to review its decision to reject 31 exhibits coming from the ECMM. The Trial Chamber does not intend to state all the -- everything that was raised by the Prosecution to support its motion nor what the Defence stated in its answer. The Trial Chamber took all this into account when ruling on this request. The Trial Chamber recalls that it will consider any request for review if the demanding party can demonstrate that the -- that in the reasoning of the impugned decision there is a genuine error or that specific circumstances can justify this decision to be reviewed in order to avoid any unfairness. In the Brix Andersen decision, among other things the Trial Chamber rejected the admission of the 31 exhibits on the grounds that the Prosecution did not abide with a previous decision made by the Trial Chamber on July 13, 2006. Prosecution did not file a written motion that would satisfy the criteria spelled out in the decision of July 13, 2006, nor did Prosecution present these documents to any witness in court. The Prosecution in its request for review did not demonstrate that the Brix Andersen decision has a manifest error, a genuine error, that would entail the rejection of the 31 exhibits. It did not demonstrate either that a review would be justified in order to avoid unfairness. The Trial Chamber would also like to recall that Prosecution waited 15 months, and I would like to underscore this figure of 15 months, after the decision was made on July 13, 2006, before it requested for these documents to be admitted. If the admission of these 31 exhibits was this essential for the Prosecution's case, it should have abided by decision of July 13, 2006. However, in its request for review, the Prosecution admits that it consciously decided to bypass this decision. Secondly, Prosecution is asking the review of a decision on the request for review of decisions rejecting the admission of 17 exhibits made on January 23, 2008, called hereunder the decision of January 23, 2008. The Trial Chamber recalls that this decision of January 23, 2008 came after a request to review two other decisions according to which the Trial Chamber had rejected the admission of 17 exhibits. This request is thus the second motion for review regarding these 17 exhibits. The Trial Chamber would also like to recall that in its decision of January 23, 2008, it noted that, and I quote: "The Prosecution obviously was not very diligent when it comes to the request to admit the elements at stake." Inasmuch that this request for review does not justify this lack of diligence that was previously noted by the Trial Chamber, there is no need to review the decision of January 23, 2008. Consequently, the Trial Chamber decides to reject the motion for review regarding the Brix Andersen decision, as well as the decision of January 23, 2008. The same applies to the request for certification of appeal given that this motion does not satisfy with the criteria spelled out on Article -- in Rule 73(B) as the Prosecution states in its submission of January 30, 2008, in its last paragraph. We now have the four oral decisions, they have been now issued, and we can move to the items that are on the agenda, but I would first give the floor to Mr. Scott. I believe he wanted the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours and to all those -- Counsel, all those in the courtroom. Thank you, Your Honour. Of course it's not the point or the purpose of the Prosecution to argue further about the Chamber's rulings just now. Only one point of clarification, and that is it was certainly, it was certainly never ever the Prosecution's intent to consciously avoid or go around a Trial Chamber decision. There have been -- the Trial Chamber throughout since this trial started in April 2006 has provided a number of different modes, a number of different routes for the admission of documentary evidence, including in connection with Rule 92 bis witnesses, and the Brix Andersen exhibits were tendered specifically by a mode of presentation that the Chamber had repeatedly instructed the Prosecution to follow, and the Prosecution had repeatedly followed it. Had we -- the Chamber has repeatedly indicated that it prefers witnesses -- excuse me, exhibits to be tendered in connection with a witness. We respected the Chamber's preference by tendering those documents through a witness, albeit not a live witness, as opposed to a written motion. Had -- to be very clear, Your Honour, had the -- had the Prosecution known what the Chamber says now, we would have filed -- sought the same admission of the same exhibits by written motion. So unfortunately it appears that the Prosecution at the end of the day has been penalised for choosing what the Chamber now considers the wrong way to do it. Had we known, they would have been tendered along with the many, many other ECMM exhibits, most of all of which were admitted and there is no distinction between these 31 exhibits and those. So unfortunately because the Prosecution did tender the exhibits pursuance to the guidance of the Trial Chamber to do as much as possible in connection with the witness, unfortunately we've now done that to our disadvantage. I regret that. Your Honour, did I ask to have a few moments of the court's time just so that I could make a couple of introductions, and I appreciate the Chamber giving me the opportunity. I need to report to the Chamber that since we last met at the conclusion of the Prosecution case two of our Prosecution team lawyers, Ms. Gillett and Mr. Flynn, have both left the ICTY to do other things with our best wishes, and that's the sad news, but the good news is we have two new lawyers who have joined the team who I want to introduce today. We have Ms. Kimberly West, a very experienced prosecutor from the United States who has joined the team, and also Hedvig Moe, who is also a very experienced prosecutor from Norway. And they are both -- we are pleased to have them join the Prosecution team. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. The Trial Chamber -- well, first was hoping all the best for Ms. Gillett and Mr. Flynn who left the ICTY, which is the best for them in their new job, and the Trial Chamber would also like to welcome Ms. Kimberly West coming from the United States. We congratulate her on working now for the OTP. And I'm sure we will soon be hearing her. We also wish the best and welcome the second person from the OTP, Ms. Moe coming from Norway, and we also congratulate her for now working for the OTP, and I'm sure that we also will soon be hearing her. It's always sad to see colleagues leave, but it's on the other hand means new colleagues are coming and that's the way things go. Now let's move to the items that are on the agenda. First let's look at the translation issue, the translation of the documents that will be shown by the Defence teams. As you know, two decisions, one of September 27, 2008, and one of January 28, 2008, the Trial Chamber decided that the Prosecution and -- that the accused and their Defence teams would disclose to the Prosecution all copies of the exhibits that they will submit but in English and on the same day as the 65 ter list, i.e., March 31st, 2008. Despite this decision, the Trial Chamber has noted that on April 11, 2008, Mr. Karnavas for Defence -- for Mr. Prlic's Defence said that he was running into difficulties regarding the translation of documents, and in its letter the Prlic Defence said that it would abide by its obligations regarding disclosure and translation. However, the Trial Chamber notes that it did not always respect its obligations, and this Trial Chamber is a bit worried about this and would like to take stock of the situation in order to know exactly where things stand regarding each Defence team, and the Trial Chamber would like to know what problems these Defence teams are experiencing. Before giving the floor to the different Defence teams, let me give you some statistics regarding the documents being translated. CLSS told us that for the Prlic Defence 3.000 -- 3.506 pages had been already been translated and that allegedly there is 937 pages still undergoing translation. Regarding the Stojic Defence, 382 pages were translated, and 36 pages are undergoing translation. Regarding the Praljak Defence, 1.990 pages were translated so far and 2.130 pages are undergoing translation. For the Petkovic Defence 570 pages have already been translated, 268 pages are still pending. For the Coric Defence 914 pages have already been translated, 271 pages are still undergoing translation. And finally for the Pusic Defence, 883 pages have been translated, and no pages are undergoing translations. So when adding all these figures up, we note that the Defence as a whole has -- stands as follows: 8.252 pages have already been translated, and as of now Defence is still waiting for 3.642 pages to be translated. When you add all this together, you end up with some 12.000 pages. What's essential for the Trial Chamber is that as soon as the first witnesses are called to testify, all documents will have to be translated into English for the OTP as well as for the Trial Chamber. Since all these Defences are going to appear in a different order, I'm sure that the CLSS will start finishing the translation for the Prlic team before working on the other pending translations. Mr. Karnavas, as far as you're concerned could you tell us exactly where you stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the court. I'm happy to dive right into this particular issue because I think that the Trial Chamber does not really fully appreciate the challenges that the Defence faces with respect to this, and in particular, this particular Defence has worked very hard from almost the very first day that I got into this case. We began meeting with the CLSS and trying to abide by their regulations, which are every time you need something translated you have to fill out a form. You have to tell them what, where, why, how. And sometimes, I must say their requests are utterly ridiculous, such as we should only be translating documents which we are absolutely 100 per cent sure we are going to be using in court. Name my one lawyer, name me one good lawyer, name me one professional lawyer who has any experience in the courtroom who can say with any degree of certainty that each and every page is going to be admitted. Simply that's not how it's done. Now, our particular Defence has translated approximately one-third, one-third of all the documents. We've done that on our own, recognising the challenges that they meet, even though we should not have to do that. The UN should provide. The UN decided to open up this Tribunal. The UN decided to allow prosecutors to have these very large indictments, and so the UN should provide the facilities necessary for translations because these cases cannot be done without those sorts of services but we've done approximately one-third of that on our own. Now, we -- when the Prosecution began its case, they had designated 9.490 documents. That was their initial 65 ter list. Thirteen per cent had not been translated, 1.248. We did not complain. We did not complain because we knew and we had expected that when the time came for the certain documents that were not translated, when that time came to be -- for those documents to be -- to be introduced in the courtroom they would be, and in fact the Prosecution met its burden, met its obligation with respect to those documents. And what I'm saying is that no case can begin with these sorts of numbers of documents where everything is translated in advance, and in fact the number that originally was given to us by the Prosecution grew, and it grew to no fault of their own, but it's the nature of the beast. They collect more documents. They search through more archives. Witnesses that they've met on several occasions all of a sudden come up at the last minute with diaries and with other sorts of documentation which they have an obligation to look at and disclose. Often those documents need to be translated, in fact most of the time. So we went along without complaining, but that is the nature of the beast in this particular case. Now, with respect to our documents, we had projected but -- that by the time we would begin our case all -- most if not all of the documents would have been translated. Unfortunately, Mr. President, when you issued an order to CLSS with respect to three other teams, they took that and they interpret that order to mean that those teams had priority over the Prlic Defence even though those teams do not go first. And so since the beginning of April, no documents are being translated by them; for us that is. We've had several exchanges of e-mails. They want us to prioritise. We prioritised. They want us to prioritise the prioritisation and it's an ongoing battle. So we've taken it upon ourselves again hiring private translators to assist us, but we're doing the work of the CLSS and they should be doing it, not us, and we're trying to accommodate. I believe you will need to issue an order to CLSS to get them to start translating and do their job for this particular Defence team who is going first. Now, as I've indicated in my letter, which was prompted by a comment, Well, in a perfect world all of these things, yes, but we're not a perfect world, and so I wanted to set out the facts how this imperfect world really works and the facts are in the letter. But be that as it may if all the other teams are going to be given priority then those other teams should go first, plain and simple. You can't have the first team not having priority in translations, especially when we began through day one. I don't know about the other teams, but we haven't waited until the very last moment. But as I've indicated in my letter, and I'll state this again and I'm sure professional, experienced counsel will verify, that in these sorts of cases it is expected that we will get additional documents, more documents. Witnesses are coming up with -- with more documents. We're finding more documents in the field. We cannot help that. We're not working off a dossier. It would be nice, but that's not the case. This is an adversarial system. But as I've indicated in my letter, I do not see any reason why anyone in this courtroom will be prejudiced because the documents that we need for the first witnesses will have been translated. They are translated I'm told. And the ones that have not been translated will be available with enough time, sufficient time, for the parties to go through them, analyse them, and prepare their respective cross-examinations. So we're not trying to either hide the ball or -- or disadvantage anyone. And incidentally when a document is in Croatian and I need to work off of that document, it doesn't help me if it's in Croatian. You know, my colleague Ms. Tomanovic can use it, but basically I need it in English as well, so I'm at equal disadvantage. With respect to the video clips, because there was an issue about that, as I understand it, what we are -- what we're doing is we're trying to isolate from hours and hours of video portions which are relevant and portions which we only intend to introduce and have those available and translated for the convenience of everyone. We do not intend to translate everything or to just ask everyone to look through the entire video but, rather, we're just going to isolate the portions which we believe are necessary and essential to our defence and make those available in a manner in which is user-friendly for all and convenient to the Trial Chamber. We want to be as efficient as we possibly can. So right now as we stand we have 347 pending translations including books and notebooks. CLSS has not sent us any translations since 3 April 2008, except for a one-page translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me if I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 347, is that pages or is it documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you give an indication as to the number of pages which is the currency in which we deal in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's the 900. I prefer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- using pages myself, but -- but it's in the 900 vicinity. Since then we have uploaded 36 new translations via documents, and all of them have been translated by the Prlic Defence team. So we're not overtaxing, overburdening poor CLSS. And that's around 300 pages. Four more will be uploaded today, approximately 70 pages. So as you can see, Mr. President and Your Honours, we are carrying more than our load to make sure that we're prepared at a considerable cost and effort to our team, because finding good -- good translators, pushing them hard to be accurate and from one's own expense can be rather taxing. We have delivered 42 video clips including the materials delivered today. Eight more need to be delivered. So that's where we stand, Mr. President, but I could -- I just want to end by saying that I pride myself and my colleague Ms. Tomanovic prides herself on being fully prepared. We intend to be fully prepared. We want to make sure that nobody is inconvenienced, and I'm rather confident, confident that barring some force majure we're going to be prepared and we're going to be efficient, and you will have all the translations in adequate time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Stojic Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I can say very briefly that the Defence counsel for Mr. Stojic will certainly have all the documents that it will be using in the course of its case translated when we begin to produce our evidence. I would also like to make a very important point, and that is that the Defence counsel for Mr. Stojic throughout the cross-examination and in preparations for the 65 ter witnesses also utilised its internal resources and translation teams, because we were aware of the possibility of having difficulties with the translation, and we are quite confident that we will complete that before we start our case. I wish also to point out that the expert witness will be the joint expert for all counsel, an expert on constitutional law, has -- was appointed as an expert on the 14th of March this year, so that quite a number of documents linked to his testimony have been disclosed rather late. These are quite lengthy documents, and we will do our best to establish with the expert with precision which pages he will be referring to so that we do not necessarily have to have all the books translated. I think that we will be able to complete this work. We're very sorry that we come second. Our team was probably preoccupied with our own problems, so we were not aware of the problems encountered by Mr. Prlic's counsel, and this Defence team feels it would be correct to advise the translation service to first undertake translations of documents of Mr. Prlic, because he will be the first to present his case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic for Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, I would like to join in the comments made regarding the overall situation with my learned friend Mr. Karnavas. We agree that the problems with the CLSS are very serious. There are a number of difficulties, and it is my personal opinion on the basis of my experience with that section of this institution that the conditions and standards of that section are quite unacceptable. This section believes that they should translate only what is evidence, and this is absurd, of course. For something to become evidence we first need to have it in one of the official languages of this Tribunal, that is in English or French for something to qualify for tendering into evidence. But that is the situation that we cannot influence. We have done our best to adjust to it, and we stand where we are now. To be more specific, the Defence for General Praljak, on the list for 65 ter witnesses handed on the 31st of March, 2008, included 625 documents which have not been translated. These are documents in the Croatian language. As the translations are arriving slowly from the CLSS, we have in the meantime received another 41 documents translated, so that on our 65 ter list now there are 584 documents left that have still not been translated. At the rate at which CLSS is providing translations, I see a potential problem there, but things are as they are. We had earlier on requested from the Chamber that it bring its influence to bear on the CLSS to speed up its work, but this is something that is still under review by the Chamber. As for the total number of pages which have been handed in for translation for the entire case and specifically for General Praljak, for the record I wish to confirm that the figures given are correct. Almost 2.000 pages have been translated by the CLSS so far, and about 2.000 and something, I think 2.100, are still in the process of being translated. Allow me to make an observation regarding these standards. I had been prompted by the query put by Judge Trechsel. The terms used by the CLSS are pages. That is so many pages, what we use as a -- normally describe as a journalist page. It's not even a full page. When we write our page has far more words than theirs. So in my view this is a rather bureaucratic approach which statistically increases the number of pages. What we as lawyers are interested in is the number of documents. For me it is quite irrelevant, and I believe also for you, Your Honours, the other counsel, and the Prosecution. Whether a document has 7, 12, or 3 pages, that is irrelevant. What matters is the document itself, whether it's short or long. So on our 65 ter list we have the number of documents. This also applies to the Prosecution. So we're interested in the number of documents. Of course I agree that at times there are documents that are like reports which can consist of many pages and we may not be interested in everything, and as the Prosecution has done, we will act similarly and have only the relevant portions translated, which is quite reasonable. Secondly, as comparing the total number of documents, according to the data you have received from the CLSS there's a total of 12.000 pages have so far been translated by them for all the Defence cases. This is just a little more of 3.000 documents, because on average each consists of about 3.3 pages, and we've reached that average on the basis of a sample taken. So this would mean a little over 3.000 documents. Let me remind you that the Prosecution on its 65 ter list had 10.000 documents. So the six defendants have encumbered the CLSS with one-third of the amount of documents already translated by the Prosecution. The difference, of course, being that we also use many of the documents of the Prosecution which have already been translated and which have been included on our 65 ter list but which the Prosecution has not yet tendered into evidence. May I also add something further. This Defence team, in our conversations with the CLSS and the Registry in general, we have been communicating very intensively since the summer of 2006. When we said that we would have a large number of statements which we had planned to tendered under 92 bis, the CLSS resolutely refused to translate statements, relying on the theory I mentioned a moment ago that this was not evidence. Then we reached a compromise solution, and that is that summaries should be translated, and the CLSS has done that. A part by -- was done by them, another part by us. And when I produced them, that is the moment I put them on the list of witnesses under 65(D) and (G). So after the Pre-Defence Conference, we know that according to the Rules I can now say to the Registry these are statements on the list. The list has formally been tendered to the Chamber. Now please have them translated. Now, what will happen with them, I don't know. I can't guarantee for anyone. I wish also to point out, as other counsel have mentioned, that during the Prosecution case a large number of documents, I don't have the exact figures now, but I think that in our report we gave the exact figure. I think one-third of the documents used during the proceedings were translated by us. Your Honours, you saw yourself that in the right-hand corner there was the indication "Unofficial office translation," and this is something we will to do in the future too if we have difficulties, but our resources are limited, and I really don't know if we'll be able to manage all that. But it is a fact that we are not receiving the support which we should be given according to the Statute. And I appeal to the Chamber once again to contact -- to establish contact with the Registry and to try to do something in this respect. Finally, I wish to say that CLSS functions on the assumption that this is one of the cases that they are translating for, and there are certain limits, certain numbers of pages, I think 200 per Defence team per month, whereby the fact is being ignored that some cases, and this one specifically, simply cannot be fitted into the statistics because in terms of their volume and scope and therefore also in terms of documents are far larger than others and require a different technical approach. And this is a fact that will into be accepted. The same limit is set for each defendant in this court, and I think that the Prosecution has a different limit, but I don't know that because it hasn't been formally verified. We will continue to work with the CLSS, and we have already submitted all the documents to them. Here and there we tend to speed up a priority of a document and that's all we can done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone. My explanation will be very short. First of all regarding the translated documents. The Defence for General Petkovic has organised translations as follows: We have established how many pages the CLSS can translate by the deadline that the Trial Chamber has set for filing the translations, and we have entrusted that number of pages to them, whereas all the others we have having translated ourselves; that is, we are paying translators. Some of these are in The Hague, some are in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If this translation process evolves according to plan, we expect to have all our documents translated by the time our case begins, and we have already disclosed some of the documents to our learned friends from the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber so that so far we have 137 documents translated. Another observation, and here I join my learned friend Ms. Nozica, in connection with the translations for Mr. Prlic's Defence. I really do not see any justified reason for any priorities being given for Stojic, Petkovic, and Coric, because the Trial Chamber has requested that Defence counsel indicate which documents will not be translated by the 31st or 3rd, and if the Defence of Mr. Prlic had made that statement then they would have been included. So could an appeal be addressed to the CLSS that priority be given to Mr. Prlic's documents, and we will adjust to that situation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. On behalf of Mr. Coric's defence, I can say the following: Last time I had informed the Trial Chamber that our team has on its team two translators for the very reason that the CLSS of this Tribunal cannot meet our requests in due time. According to the last information that I have, the CLSS will translate another 127 documents for Mr. Coric, and 48 documents will not be translated by the due date. The 48 documents have been forwarded to our translators on the team, and they will also be translated by the deadline, which is the 26th of May. And now given the situation with the Prlic Defence and with the fact that they are to go first and that it is understandable that the priorities should be changed in light of that fact, at this moment I cannot guarantee that all of our documents will be translated before the 26th of May, but I'm sure that they will be translated much sooner than the start of the Coric Defence case. As far as the documents are concerned that were put on our list and were not translated and have been translated in the meantime, the translations are now in e-court, and our learned friends from the other Defence teams and the Prosecution have been informed, as well as has been the Trial Chamber, and we will put a binder in a hard copy for the Trial Chamber with all our translations when all of them are completed. Just to avoid any confusion we will have a binder containing all the translated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As far as our translation are concerned, we met our obligation on the 31st of March. I have nothing to add. I appreciate that other Defence teams do have problems with the translations, and I hope that these will be resolved before their Defence cases start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. When I didn't have a lawyer because of the problems with funding, I knew what would have to be translated and we started sending documents for translations already two or three years ago. Those documents were returned, and people from the CLSS called me once, twice, or three times a day every time pointing out some difficulties and ordering me how to write these documents. We had good computer programmes, and every time they were surprised that we were able to circumvent the difficulties that they saw in our documents. However, Your Honour, you called this case yourself the biggest trial in the history of the international justice. It seems that we are on a green market at which the CLSS orders both the Trial Chamber and us, the accused, what our right is. It seems to me that we have a paper here saying what our rights are with regard to translation. If the Defence has reduced the number of witnesses to 10 per cent of the number of witnesses that I wanted to bring here, which was 220, it seems to me that it would only be fair for the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber to have their statements. The indictment covers a lot of years. It deals with psychology and psychology, and a system cannot be closed with pieces of papers relating to just a short period of time. Mr. -- Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, can you please allow me to finish what I have to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but please hurry, because this is a problem that we know very well, and your lawyer explained it to us already. So please accelerate. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for an answer as to what is the right of the accused and their Defence counsel for the documents to be translated at the beginning of their cases. What is the right of the Chamber to issue orders, and what is the position of the CLSS in the Tribunal? Are they those that execute orders or do they issue orders themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your counsel will be in a position to answer that particular question. Let me remind you that the Trial Chamber issued a decision on the 28th of March, 2008, following a request by Mr. Stojic, Petkovic, and Coric related to the translation of various documents. In that decision we stated that we requested that translations be provided by the 26th of May, 2008, at the latest. In other words, by this decision the Trial Chamber clearly stated that everything should be translated by the date of 26th of May, 2008. We are going to take stock of the situation once again with the CLSS. We are going to try and find out if that deadline will be complied with or not. The Defence exhibits, as Prosecution exhibits, should be translated. That's the rule. And as you know, an exhibit can be admitted into evidence only if it's been translated into one of the two working languages of the Tribunal. That's the right -- right you have. You have the right to ask for a document to be admitted, and that's why when the document has not been shown with the translation an MFI number is given before the document is translated. The only problem that the CLSS raised is that they do not want to translate every single document, any document, and they want this document to be shown at trial for admission, because otherwise you could ask for thousands of books to be translated, and that would be a disaster for the CLSS. The situation is serious, but it's not without hope, and I believe that we'll manage to find a solution very soon. That's my wish, but as I said, we are going to get in touch with the translation service. We are going to ask them to provide us with a report on the way things stand. That's the only response I can give you at this stage. Now let me move on to the third point on the agenda for today. It's something that we added to the agenda following a filing by the Prosecution that had identified a number of inconsistencies. Witness list 1D. The Prosecution noted, but we had noted it of course ourselves earlier. It was noted that Prlic -- the Accused Prlic was not on the list, whereas during the 65 ter Conference Mr. Karnavas told us that Mr. Prlic would testify it. The Trial Chamber would like to know several things. First of all, is Mr. Prlic going to testify? Secondly, as an exploratory question, the Chamber would like to know the following: If Mr. Prlic is going to testify, when is he going to testify? Would he testify in the middle of the Prlic Defence case, or did you consider, as the other Defence teams, did you consider having all the accused testify at the end of the trial once all the other witnesses have testified? Then the accused could all testify at the end. Another question we want to ask you: If Mr. Prlic testifies, how many hours will that take? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again good afternoon, Mr. President. There's no need to be alarmed why he wasn't on the list. He is an accused. He is not a witness. That's why he wasn't put on the list. I thought I'd made it very clear that he would be testifying, but if that caused any confusion, my apologies to anyone who was confused about that. With respect to the order, as I had indicated where we thought we would have Dr. Prlic testify initially in light of what we believed might be the wishes of the Trial Chamber, we then heard from the Bench where you indicated that you would prefer he would go last. We assumed that you meant last in our case. That was fine with us. With respect to this new invitation, I would like to consult with Dr. Prlic first before I would speak on his behalf, but I think it is an interesting proposition. But in any event, to the extent that we can get these judicial hints, we appreciate them, because we certainly want to do things that make the Trial Chamber -- would make its job most efficient and beneficial. So we thank you. Perhaps we can get back to you on that answer after the break. Oh, as far as how many hours. As far as how many hours, well, I believe I had calculated at one point, and it was -- it came out to approximately 24 hours by our calculation. Now, that could be a little bit less, it could be a little bit more, but probably on the lesser side. But that's how -- I recall when Mr. Krajisnik testified, and we have someone who was here who -- who did participate in those events, the gentleman was on the stand for several weeks. I believe it was seven or eight or maybe ten weeks, somewhere near that. I know that others have testified in the vicinity of three to four weeks in total. We have to keep in mind that this is a document case, and there are a lot of documents that we need to go through. The minutes of the meetings. There was all sorts of reports that were introduced such as the Tomljanovich report, this expert report that discussed all sorts of things. So given that, it seems to me that we would need to spend a great deal of time. Now, having said that, the Trial Chamber will have had the benefit by that point, assuming that Dr. Prlic goes last, even after our case, would have had the benefit of hearing from several members of the -- the HVO executive authority, and so it may be that certain areas you would tell us that you were sufficiently apprised of that topic and did not need to hear any testimony on, so that might shorten it a bit. But what I would expect, Your Honours, is that prior to Dr. Prlic testifying is providing you with a rather detailed outline of the topics so you would know which order we were going to cover the topics. It would be sort of an outline that would help you. And so then in the event you want us to of move to another particular topic or if the order switched we would accommodate you in that fashion. And that will of course be provided to the Prosecution in advance as well so that they could prepare their cross-examination, though I'm sure Mr. Scott is preparing already as we speak. And I see him shaking his head like a good advocate. I hope I answered your questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Yes. You've answered my question indeed. Now with respect to the Praljak Defence, the Trial Chamber, you will not be surprised to hear, has reviewed the summaries, the names of the witnesses given, and we noted the following, and the Prosecution saw that too: In many cases their summaries are not precise enough or not accurate enough, and we have a lack of detail of -- about the time period these witnesses are talking about. It's all very vague. It's all very vague. We are a bit -- we lack some certainty. But on my own personal behalf I'll say the following: With respect to the list of witnesses for Mr. Praljak, the question at stake is the following: These witnesses will come and testify. Will they talk about the events at the end of 1992 before what happened in Prozor? Then there is the period of six months in 1993 about which we do not know exactly what was Mr. Praljak's position or situation. Then we have the period of July to November. Mr. Praljak is in office because he was appointed commander of the HVO. Then around the 8th of November Mr. Praljak left the scene. And considering this, I have the feeling that in this 65 ter list we have a mix. We have no idea who is going to come and testify for what purpose, and there is a lack of specification, Mr. Kovacic. We need to have more detail. Can you please answer this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- Your Honours, I would be ready, but that would take a lot of time if we went from one witness to another, but if you have any uncertainties about that, about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm expecting a general kind of a summary, a few minutes of response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In principle I can tell you. The witnesses -- actually their summaries are primarily distributed around various events. For example, there's a group of witnesses that will testify about the events in Prozor. As we all know, Prozor is a count in the indictment. There are certain dates of incriminating events, and the witnesses will be talking about these events in Prozor. I don't think that the summaries should show the times. The time is relevant, because in Prozor some things happened before the incriminating events and some happened after the incriminating events. First and foremost we're interested in the location. That is our theme around which our witnesses are centred. That's one principle. The second principle resolves around some other terms, for example, subordination, or the third group of witness will come to testify about the events at the beginning of the war, at the time when the HVO and the Territorial Defence were engaged in common defence operations and their break-up. So this is more or less clear. But if you wish any further clarification, we are at your disposal. In time we can give you further clarifications. My client has something to add, but I have to tell you that he has prepared most of the witnesses himself when he had not been appointed a Defence counsel. Maybe he can provide you with some more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is true that the summaries had been done in haste. It did arise that these witnesses have not been grouped, but they will come in groups and the criterion is very simple. The criterion is temporal which means that witnesses will talk about certain periods of the time. There will be character witnesses, very few of them, there are witnesses talking about what I did before the war, what I did during the war in Croatia to display how the accused behaved in that period, and then there will be some to talk about what I did in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we did not have the general part of the indictment for joint criminal enterprise, I would then focus only on the periods when I was in charge of things that would obviously carry a certain amount of responsibility. However, since we are part of the joint indictment, I had to extend my list of witnesses to cover all the counts of indictment meaning the functioning of the Croatian state, when it comes to logistics, the military, the transport, harbours, arms, because as an officer of the Croatian army and the assistant minister of defence for psychological and information matters, I had a certain amount of influence and responsibility. I participated in all that, and I know about these things. I know how the -- the BiH army was armed. I know how we prepared the Geneva Conventions for all the soldiers on the front line, primarily the HVO soldiers, which means that I have called all those witnesses who will speak about what I did during that period and to testify whether the indictment is correct or not. They will talk about the psychological, military, and material aspect of my work. They will talk about very minute details to show what the life was really like and avoid creating an unrealistic world that will not reflect what was really happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Things have been clarified somewhat with respect to your witnesses. Now let's move on to 4D. The Petkovic Defence has not stated how they would present their witnesses. We have the feeling that 4D will call all its witnesses viva voce, whereas in the Rules you can have viva voce witnesses but also 92 ter or 92 bis witnesses. That's provided for by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This is the reaction of the Prosecution, but I must say that myself, when I reviewed the 4D witness list, I came to the same conclusion. My question to the Petkovic Defence is whether they will only call their witnesses viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was our intention to have only viva voce witnesses. We believed that on the list that we have where we have shown how much time we want to spend in direct examination this list shows that these are witnesses that we want to hear viva voce. When compiling our list we tried to be as concise and rational as possible. We did not want to bring these witnesses that would be repetitive that will be talking about same topics and saying more or less the same things and that's why we believe we are lacking one of the important elements, which is presenting evidence through 92 bis and ter evidence, because we're talking about the cumulative evidence of all the witnesses. We believe that when estimating the time we were also very rational. We have tried avoid trading time and trying to ask for more than we actually need. We have tried to be rational and respect limits in the number of witnesses and the amount of time, and we tried to present all those things that will be relevant for the Trial Chamber in terms of the facts and evidence that we wish to present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've shed some light on the situation, on the reason why you want viva voce witnesses to be called in your case, but now we have another issue we need to raise. That's the issue of expert witnesses and joint witnesses. I have a confession to make. When I reviewed your witnesses, all witnesses, all the Defence teams, there's something that I didn't quite understand. I don't understand who will be the expert witnesses common to all the Defence teams, and who will be the other witnesses, the other joint witnesses, who will come and testify on behalf of all six accused. Let me give you some explanation about this based on a table prepared by the Trial Chamber, but we need to move into private session because I'm going to give the names of protected witnesses. We need to move into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Sorry, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if you were to look, for instance, at our witness list, I'm shocked and surprised that my colleagues didn't identify members of the Presidency of BiH to put on their list to talk about what was happening in Sarajevo or that they don't have any witnesses to talk about international negotiations. Perhaps they felt that others would deal with that issue. If you look at those -- some of the other lists, you'll see that they're targeted to their particular case. Fine. Our defence is based on first and foremost that there is a joint criminal enterprise. And it doesn't matter if somebody is your subordinate who commits the particular crime. If it's a natural and foreseeable consequence of the events and you're a member of the joint criminal enterprise, well, then you share in the responsibility. At least that's my understanding of the law. And maybe I misunderstand the law, but I believe that's how it works. So when I say that witnesses benefit everyone, I think it is to everyone's benefit that we have these witnesses. Now, whether they choose to cross-examine them, that's fine. They could do direct examination. That's fine, too, through their cross or through open-ended questions, it's all up to them, but we have no common expert witnesses on our list. Now, there was one witness that's on the Stojic Defence that's an expert we have met. That witness you could say is common because there is some coordination, and Ms. Nozica is taking the lead. I presume that when the gentleman comes that we would be able to assist Ms. Nozica in preparing him and that in the time that she has asked if there are areas which we think that might be relevant that she would ask them. If not, we might be given leave to ask some additional questions, but that's a common witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, yes, but you have just raised a problem that I had not envisaged in the first place and that has just cropped up, this question of proofing. You're saying that there's a witness that will be proofed with Ms. Nozica. So if I understood you well, all witnesses for all parties will be proofed individually with the lawyer of only one accused, but there might be witnesses which will be jointly proofed. Is that the way it's going to work?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I want to disabuse anyone of the notion that there is a joint effort or a joint enterprise, leaving out the criminal aspect of it, because I don't think we engage in criminality, but there is no joint enterprise between us and we haven't sat around to talk about it. If there is a common witness, I envisage, such as an expert witness, where I am coordinating with Ms. Nozica, just to use this as an example, I would know in advance which documents and which areas she is going to cover. It's a joint witness. She is going to be conducting the direct examination. Certainly I would like the opportunity to be invited during the preparation and to have my input since it's a common witness. I think it's -- that's sort of natural. Whether that would occur or not, I don't know. Now, for instance, if there is a witness that somebody brings up, an expert witness but is not a common witness, I intend to cross-examine if there is a need and only if there is need. But if there is a need, I will cross-examine with leading questions, and the witness may be treated in a hostile manner. Not hostile -- in the sense of asking leading questions, not with hostility. No pun intended. But so -- so I just want to make sure, Your Honour, the problem is we have six different teams. One of the reasons -- for instance, in the Praljak list you'll see that they have 92 bis and now they've asked for 15 minutes. It's because they've gone out, I assume, taken a statement. Now they see somebody who they have the statement and is going to be live in court giving viva voce testimony. Well, it then behooves them to ask viva voce questions to either supplement that statement or to get the statement in, or in lieu of the statement to have the viva voce testimony. I think that's how I think that occurred is because there's been no coordination. But there's been no coordination because we're distinct Defence teams. And it's not because we don't like each other or that we don't trust each other, but we have our respective clients, and our clients give us instructions. We come from different legal traditions. We have different strategies, different approaches, but I can assure you that there have been some efforts, at least early on, to have some sort of coordinated effort, and we've done that to a large extent through motion practice where we were able to assist the Trial Chamber by filing joint motions, but at this stage we're at a very critical stage and we certainly don't wish to be seen as some sort of a joint defence ganging up on the Prosecution even though they probably have a lot more resources than we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, still going to the issue of proofing, is it a matter of the Chamber to address it at all, or is it something that we should entirely leave to the Defence? If, for instance, we have (redacted) and where Mr. Praljak or the Praljak Defence also wants to ask some questions, isn't it entirely up to them whether they do proofing together or separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I agree with you, but we're in open session so perhaps we shouldn't be mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're absolutely correct. And I think that to the extent -- I mean we're all colleagues and I don't think there's going to be a problem on that. But I think you're absolutely right. It's up to us. Of course the person who is calling the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We'll move back into private session, because if we start mentioning witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I can --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: We're now open session, but perhaps I can just check that the witness's name that was inadvertently mentioned previously, has an order been made for redaction? I presume it has. I see from the court officer an order has not been made for redaction. I do apply that that witness's name be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please prepare the order because we have 30 minutes. Yes, Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. It is page 41, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. If I must say something else. We discussed this during the break. A double expert witness that appears as a joint witness, I won't mention the name, we mentioned him a moment ago, as a joint expert of all Defence counsels. In the submission of the 14th of April we said that we would use the advantage when he is present to refer to a separate event. We had planned him as 92 bis. I am letting you know that we will not do this so as not to affect the expert witness's testimony, because that would dilute his testimony. We can refer to that incident through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will explain very briefly that we do have a joint expert witness for constitutional law. He is the expert mentioned by Ms. Nozica. And for the Defence of General Praljak we have a joint expert for military issues. And may I now be allowed to say a few sentences regarding experts and witnesses regarding joint criminal enterprise that has been discussed by colleague Karnavas. I wish in particular to clarify certain points to as to avoid any misunderstandings. In the Prosecution case we saw that Mr. Prlic's defence focused mostly on the joint criminal enterprise issues and not the call -- so-called base issues. And Mr. Karnavas has already said that he will mainly focus on those topics of joint criminal enterprise rather than -- and that we can focus on the crime base issues. And further to such an agreement the Defences have focused their attention on some other issues. As the Defence of General Petkovic has indicated in our list of witnesses, our witnesses also comment on the joint criminal enterprise issue. This is explicitly stated in relation to counts and paragraphs. The differences between those witnesses and the witnesses we will hear at the beginning of the Prlic case is the following: Our witnesses, in addition to joint criminal enterprise issues, will also focus on crime base issues. That is through concrete issues we will try to elaborate on joint criminal enterprise as opposed to witnesses who will be discussing exclusively joint criminal enterprise issues and other issues related to them. That is why I believe that the witnesses not only for General Petkovic and for Mr. Prlic, that all these witnesses to a greater or lesser degree also deal with the issue of joint criminal enterprise. We do not have joint experts or witnesses with Mr. Prlic's Defence simply because no one was proposed to us as a joint witness, but we believe that in future preparations and possibly through cross-examination, we will be able to discuss issues which are of interest to all the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very brief. The Defence for Mr. Coric has one joint witness and that is the expert on Mr. Stojic's list. And as far as we know, he's the joint expert of all Defence teams as proposed by Ms. Nozica. In addition to that witness, and we have already explained this in our filings about the witnesses that appear on several lists, there's a witness who appears as a viva voce expert on our list and on the list of the 6D Defence, and both we and the 6D Defence have informed the Chamber that our intention is that this witness be examined during the testimony for Mr. Coric, and first the counsel for Mr. Coric will examine him and then Mr. Pusic's Defence, because I think we are questioning him about different issues. I think that is in accordance with the instructions of the Trial Chamber. In addition, we have two other witnesses who appear on the -- on Mr. Prlic's defence and Mr. Praljak's defence lists as 92 bis witnesses. As for the technical approach to their examination, I agree that what is practical is what Ms. Nozica has said, but similarly, there is the risk that colleague Kovacic has referred to, so that I would suggest that the Chamber consider both these methods of examination, which are the advantages and disadvantages, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber will find the best solution. As for the circumstances that our witnesses will be testifying about, I don't think we need to go into that because our list contains a summary of the statements and refers to the counts and paragraphs that these witnesses will be testifying about so that it is clear from those lists what these witnesses will be testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And now Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't wish to repeat what has already been said by my colleagues. Mr. Coric's Defence has already explained our joint position regarding a joint witness, and we have another two witnesses who should testify viva voce, and also on Mr. Praljak's 92 bis list. Maybe a practical solution would be when we call these witnesses then the -- other Defence teams can, through the cross-examination, obtain what they wanted through 92 bis, because there's a question as to whether they will be accepted or not. I don't know what Mr. Kovacic's position is. Should we not be calling those witnesses, then we would inform Mr. Praljak's Defence for those statements to be admitted, and that would avoid the risk that Mr. Kovacic has referred to. Thank you. Mr. Chairman, just one further observation. Regarding the two witness that the Prosecution has asked whether they will be expert witness or regular witnesses, they have academic titles but they will be testifying as regular witnesses, not as expert witnesses. They are two doctors, specialists, who will be talking about specific problems, exhumation, pathological findings, and other issues that have arisen during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add a comment to the subject we have dealt with now. I think in the beginning the idea was that if we -- if you take this list it's always the team that comes first which has invoked the witness that will bring this witness. Now, if you look -- if we look at the list, you will see that there are witnesses where the Pusic Defence has three hours, four hours, and the Praljak Defence has 15 minutes, so that it seems that it is mainly a witness of the -- of the Pusic team. And one may wonder whether that in case the -- it is more or less in second lieu a witness for the Praljak Defence and in first line a witness for the Pusic Defence. Then it may be more convenient if the Pusic Defence calls him and the supplementary questions come at that moment. I just draw your attention to this. I think it's up to you to agree, but it's -- it's a consideration that might be worthy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to talk about another topic. The Prosecution in their writing asked that the Defence give tables of witnesses and of evidence. On the 4th of September, 2006, the Prosecution at the request of the Chamber had produced this chart enabling to criss-cross the information between the witnesses and the evidence. The Chamber thus request as the Defence indicates on that list of exhibits what is the witness that they -- through which witness, rather, they wish to present evidence. The Trial Chamber, in the guidelines that it will produce tomorrow or after tomorrow is going to request that when a party present a witness they inform the Trial Chamber two weeks prior to the hearing of the witness and -- and gives the Trial Chamber the list of exhibits that they wish to show during the hearing, and thanks to the name of the witness and the list of exhibits, we will have 15 days before a witness appears. The Prosecution, just as the Trial Chamber, will have those elements of information, that information, enabling the Trial Chamber to establish a link between the exhibits, the witness, and the paragraphs on the indictment. So the Trial Chamber believes that at this stage it is not mandatory that the Defence present this chart, because we will be able to have -- 15 days prior to the arrival of the witness we will be able to establish the link between witnesses, exhibits, and indictment. This is what we wished to tell you. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. There's a couple of matters I would like to be heard on, and I don't want to necessarily take all the Chamber's time now, but I do note that we're on -- we appear to be on agenda item 5 or 6 of the Trial Chamber's agenda from last Thursday or Friday when it was circulated. Some of our comments, Your Honour, would be brief, but based on prior experience with all respect I'm concerned that if the Prosecution is not heard as we go on different agenda items we will approaching 7.00 and the Prosecution will be faced with playing catch up on all the items today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is why I'm going fast. So at this point in time you would like to intervene to tell us what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. On this particular point and then I'll be in the Chamber's hands whether you want to go back to some of the prior topics or not, but on this particular point, Your Honour, I think the most important thing about the additional element on the charts that we did not find on the existing Defence charts was the information that was required not only the linkage to the paragraph and the witness but also the information in terms of source and indicia of reliability and in order that we can prepare for each witness, we would ask that what the Chamber has just described as the two-week or 15-day chart just as the Prosecution was required to fill out that information, that that information also be required concerning Defence exhibits, for example, whether they came from the Croatian State Archive, whether they came from an international organisation, what have you, but that appears to us to be missing in the listings so far, and we would ask the Chamber to add that to the requirements. I would -- I would like, Your Honour, to go back -- I'm not going to go all the way back unless the Chamber invites me to do so, but I would like to go back to the issue we were just talking about just so there there's no misunderstanding about this issue of examination and cross-examination. I think that the discussion has been helpful in that I think it's become clear that whether a witness on their face or on some list is expressly described as a joint or common witness, in fact, many of them are. That's what's become apparent more in the last 15, 20 minutes, half an hour. In fact they are closely related. In fact they all relate to JCE, some of them do. There are a number of common witnesses. It's perhaps out of an abundance of caution but if I heard the President a few minutes ago correctly and if the translation is correct, the reference was used to -- when the other Defence conduct a cross-examination of the witness and, Your Honour, that would be a concern that we have. If it's a joint witness or interest -- with common interest the Prosecution would not consider that to be a cross-examination in the sense of hostile questioning or leading questions. That is indeed a common witness and we would not believe it would be appropriate for the Prlic accused, for example, Defence to call a witness, put its direct examinations and for other Defence teams to get up and say, "Well, I didn't call this witness a common witness. I didn't call this witness. Therefore I'm going to conduct a cross-examination by leading questions, et cetera, by friendly witness." We don't think that would be appropriate. That indeed should be considered a joint and common witness with the Prosecution actual cross-examination following all Defence questioning. Now, as we said in our papers, we do allow, of course, we do allow that there may be some instances in which you could truly have an adverse witness. For example, if hypothetically speaking, Mr. Prlic and Mr. Karnavas were to call a witness on Mr. Prlic's behalf but that witness happens to say -- who do I pick on? That it was actually Mr. Petkovic who was responsible for this course of conduct. Well, then indeed the Petkovic Defence team's cross-examination of that witness on that point would be adverse and presumably might be a subject for cross-examination. That would be a -- that would be a true example of cross-examination. But follow-up questions or additional questions by other Defence teams to -- to a Defence witness, Your Honour, we do not submit, would be -- that's not cross-examination being conducted in a different way such as leading questions in what might be called a more hostile approach, and we wanted to make that very clear that that's the Prosecution position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may just briefly rebut that point. Here's the -- here's the problem that that poses: First of all, not everyone is going to be proofing that particular witness and I think that if you're going to be asking open-ended questions, you know: The who, what, where, why, how, explain, describe, which is normally how you do direct examination, and you haven't had the benefit of sitting with that witness and going through the lists of questioning, I think then you ask questions at your peril because you haven't met that witness. That's why you need to cross-examine. Whereas if the witness is common in the sense and perhaps common in a way that the Defence have coordinated and have allowed an opportunity to -- to proof the witness or they've divided the areas that there will be direct examine, no problem. But I would -- I would like to reserve the right to cross-examine any witness that is being brought up, because even in an innocent fashion they may say something that I may not agree with and may be contrary to my particular defence. So with all due respect to Mr. Scott's position, I don't think that we can treat every witness as a common witness and only the rare exceptions should we be allowed to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not start a debate on this. The Trial Chamber will render its decision about guidelines. This is a theoretical debate that you are talking about. Clearly the party calling the witness will put non-leading questions, and most of the time the other Defence teams will intervene without putting leading questions, but it is quite possible that in some cases, but this should be an exception rather than the rule, that the witness, let's say, answered to questions put by the party that called him, but this could create problems for another party, another accused. So quite rightfully Defence counsel for another witness has the right to cross-examine. That's quite obvious. But the general principle adopted by the Trial Chamber, and this is what we will put in our decision that you will get shortly, one party calls a witness. The other accused may cross-examine him or her, and the Prosecution may cross-examine him or her, and that is the guideline, the general guideline. Of course we need to add that with a number of witnesses there will be no problem whatsoever for cross-examination. But as I said on many occasions, the issue of leading or non-leading questions is purely academic, because you have four professional and experienced Judges in front of you, and they know, on the basis of the question put to the witness, they know whether the question is neutral, directed, more or less directed -- directive, and believe me, the Judges are in a position to assess the value of the answer given by the witness depending on the way the question was put. It's an automatic process, and there's no need to have any concern about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not going to repeat that point, but I do before we move to another point, so I can at least complete on this topic, can I just come back and say as we've said in our papers that we filed last week we suggest again, and I think the discussions this afternoon, while helpful, have also indicated that I think it would assist everyone in the courtroom, including the Chamber, including the Prosecution, perhaps other Defence teams among themselves, if an additional filing could be made simply makes a further effort based on these discussions as to which witnesses are common. We see -- I don't dismiss the amount of work involved. Everyone knows, the Prosecution knows what it is like to put on case. We've been there. We've done it. It's burdensome. But it would assist everyone and the Chamber, especially in light of the guidance that the Chamber has given and the dialogue this afternoon if an additional table or listing could be provided jointly by all the Defence making a further effort to identify these joint or common witnesses. Number one. That's suggestion number one which we make respectfully to the Chamber. Secondly, and I say secondly because I don't see this as a substitute for number one but as an additional tool to assist everyone, including the Chamber, I believe if the Chamber gets to it we hope that the Chamber will require the Defence to do what we were required to do and that is to provide at a least a 30-day rolling trial calendar. It further seems to us, Your Honours, that when that trial calendar is put out approximately 30 days in advance, that that would be an additional -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to deal with that matter. I was going to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could -- in this specific context, Your Honour, if I could finish my thought, please. On that particular point, on that -- there would be an additional opportunity for the Defence to indicate for the next 30 days these are the common witnesses, these are the joint witnesses, and it could be put on at that table. It would assist everybody. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm -- I'm much obliged. Your Honour, I do take your comments regarding the futility of engaging in academic arguments needlessly extremely seriously. However, for the record I think it's necessary to submit that despite having the utmost respect of course to my learned friend Mr. Scott, the Defence for Bruno Stojic vigorously and fundamentally disagrees on takes issue with the contentions put forward. Your Honour, of course Your Honours do have reference to the previous Status Conference and in that, which is why I haven't repeated it on this occasion, in that the Defence of Bruno Stojic took issue with my learned friend's Mr. Karnavas's categorisation of having witnesses that are common to or useful or have utility to other Defence teams. Your Honour, these are matters that must be essentially within the province of each team taking instructions from their client. And, Your Honour, these cases are nuanced. It may well -- very well be the case that a particular witness may in some material particulars be useful to a co-accused, but similarly there may be points of divergence and of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. It is only a correction in line 2. I believe you wanted to say that "Your Honour these cases are nuanced." Now it is already appearing as a correction and because previously it was not written correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, there may well be areas in which an accused or co-accused has essential disagreement, but any attempt to foist a witness down the throats of a co-accused runs contrary, of course, to the rights of every accused that's stands before you. Your Honour, there is a huge jeopardy in calling a Defence witness. Every witness that any Defence team wishes to call may explode in that particular witness's face. One may be foisted with one's own petard. So a degree of circumspection has to be used by the Defence teams that are calling a particular witness. Your Honour, I know that in this case I know almost the entire investigative work has been done by lead counsel, and the witness list put down have been carefully selected in the interests of Mr. Bruno Stojic. Your Honour, that's the first point. Of course it may well be consistent with the Prosecution theory of the case to lump all the accused together in one JCE, but even there, Your Honour, there are these two options. A witness may be called by an accused who seeks to controvert the essential fundamentals of a JCE et al. That's obvious. Similarly it's open to an accused, open to a team, to call a witness who may not dispute the existence of a JCE but simply say Witness 1, 2, or 3 or accused 1, 2, or 3 are not part of it. So again these are matters that must be left to the discretion of a Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just -- Mr. Khan. I am not of the view that Mr. Scott had the intention to impose on Defence teams to accept certain witnesses against their will as common witnesses. Am I wrong, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. You're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So I think you fight no opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, because what Mr. Scott said very clearly was he was seeking to circumscribe the rights of an accused to cross-examine. Now, cross-examination, Your Honour, cross-examination has an extreme forensic utility to a Defence team. It has at least two advantages. Your Honours of course can -- are professional Judges and can assess the credibility of any witness before you. But, Your Honours, we do in this courtroom work under extreme constraints of time. The ability of a team to cross-examine a witness saves time. That's point number one, because questions need be -- need not be open-ended. They can be very focused specific questions in cross-examination.
