But secondly, as I understood Mr. Scott, his view, his opening parting shot was in fact the last 15, 20 minutes, the last half an hour have actually shown that there are common witnesses. Well, Your Honours, it's a matter for the Defence teams to decide which witnesses are common and which are not, and if a Defence team states these witnesses are not common, they must be entitled to cross-examine these witness if they wish to do. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've taken note of what you have stayed. The Judges will have a meeting at 7.00 p.m. and we will take comments into account when establishing the guidelines. There is a more essential item we have to deal with, it's the time. But Mr. Scott, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, one moment. Just to pick up on Judge Trechsel's comment and in light of counsel's comments just now. I do stand by my characterisation that this discussion much of the afternoon has indicated that there are indeed a number of common witnesses. I think that came clear through much of the discussion. There was even discussion of course you could come to joint proofing, of we could prepare this witness together, of course they would be common to areas of interest. So I stand by my characterisation number one. Number two. It may be a lost, I hope not to be presumptuous in saying this, but there may be a point here that in the common law system cross-examination has a particular connotation. Cross-examination is a more hostile, more aggressive leading questions, that sort thing. Cross-examination means a particular type of questioning, and it's in that sense that the Prosecution submits that in situations where there is indeed -- it is -- the witness is a common witness realistically whatever label is put on them, where they are a common interest and there has not been adverse evidence given to another accused it would not be cross-examination as that term is used specifically in the common law rightly or wrongly whether that's the best system or not, but it would not be considered cross-examination. It would be considered further questioning by the Defence. Number -- point number two and point number three, I said I would only take a moment, I thought I clearly said and again I agree with Judge Trechsel's clarification in response to my learned friend. Clearly there may be instances on where it may be adverse, and I can tell the Chamber if that happens, if Mr. Prlic's witness gets up and accuses Mr. Petkovic of doing something wrong, you will get no objection from the Prosecution for the Petkovic Defence team to cross-examine that witness adversely on that point. No objection from the Prosecution on that. That's cross-examination on an adverse point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Let's stop here. We have more essential matters to deal with. One point of clarification. Team 1D, you've filed 26 videos, but we have 34 videos on your list. Please try to identify the problem. As for the testimony of the witness -- of the accused. Mr. Prlic told us that he would be testifying. We mentioned that the last time that you have to tell us whether your client will be testifying or not. If he testifies, and you said that at the last conference, but we want to have a confirmation from Mr. Stojic first of all. Mr. Stojic, is he going to testify? Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Stojic will not testify. I am saying this at this moment, and I believe this will remain so until the end of our case. However, I reserve the right to change that should Mr. Stojic change his opinion, but we will inform the Trial Chamber in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak will be testifying. How many hours do you request?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we adhere to our previous position. Mr. Praljak is on the list of our witnesses, and we asked for 36 hours, if I'm not mistaken. This looks like a very little time, but we have taken everything into account. We limited the time of all our other witnesses to a minimum. And bearing in mind the testimonies of other accused in -- in the other cases, I believe that you will agree that this is a very modest amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment we believe that General Petkovic will testify, and the desirable time is the time that we asked for, 12 hours, and we believe it is not too much in light of the period of time that he spent in his position. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] As we've already informed you, we have not changed our opinion. Mr. Coric will testify. He is on our list, and we are asking for 15 hours for his testimony, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Pusic is not going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now let's move on to opening statements. According to Rule 84 opening statements may be made, and according to Rule 84 bis accused persons may make a statement. As for opening statements, we would like to know who will make an opening statement, and we'd like to know whether the accused will be making a statement. We'll go by the order of the teams, 1D, 2D, et cetera. Mr. Karnavas, we'll start with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I indicated last time, we see no utility in making an opening statement at this stage given that we've been in trial now for two years and you more or less know exactly what this case is about. We also believe that you through our 65 ter filing, and these proceedings, you have gotten a pretty good sense of where our case is and how it's structured. So we see no benefit in spending a day or two. Others may see that. We don't. We're not in front of a jury, we're in front of professional Judges therefore we want to go right into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. 2D, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 2D will deliver a short opening statement. For the time being we believe that it will be either me or my co-counsel. If Mr. Stojic is to deliver opening statement, we will certainly inform you in due time, because our Defence case starts after Mr. Prlic's Defence case, and we believe that this leaves plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say you're going to make a short statement. How short?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forty-five minutes is a short time in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in our earlier submission we have informed you about that, and we have asked for both opening statements. I -- the opening speech by the Defence and by the accused, according to 84 bis Rule. We ask for a total of three hours, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three hours for you and for Mr. Praljak, for the both of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the total. And if you're interested in a breakdown, I am going to spend about three-quarters of an hour, and General Praljak will use up about two and a half hours for his opening speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D4.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we plan to deliver an opening speech of about an hour or so. We would like to explain our case and give a road map to the Trial Chamber through the evidence of -- for General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Petkovic will not be taking the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this moment. We don't plan for General Petkovic to deliver a speech or a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D5. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Our plan is the same as the plan of General Petkovic Defence, a short opening speech for up to an hour. For the time being it will be me. Mr. Coric will not participate in that. If there are any changes, we will inform you thereof in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, our plan has not changed, which means there will be an opening statement for up to an hour and a half, and Mr. Pusic has not been planned to deliver any opening statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me move on to another topic now. I'm not asking you to comment on what I'm going to say because we would then be wasting a great deal of time. The Judges have considered the matter and as things stand our position is the following: When the accused testify, whilst they are sitting there in front of you, one week, two weeks, three weeks, four weeks, five weeks, we don't know, throughout that time, throughout the testimony of the accused, the Trial Chamber, and that's my personal opinion in particular, I believe that the link between the accused and his counsel should not be broken. I believe that the accused should be in a position to consult his counsel. If the parties have a view on the matter, but we're not there yet, but if you have a particular view on this file something in writing, if you're against that or not. Please tell us what you believe about that, about the right of the accused to have contact with his counsel whilst testifying. If you think that you should give your views to the Chamber about this, please put that in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add the following: I believe that it is a matter of interest for the accused and the Defence counsel. The Trial Chamber should not intervene in the matter. I believe in particular that the Trial Chamber should not issue any order one way or the other. I believe that it is your responsibility and your responsibility alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You understand what is at stake here. You know that other Trial Chambers have adopted a different stand. If you want to file submissions, please feel free to do so. Let's move on to the schedule of the witnesses. Tomorrow or the day after tomorrow the Trial Chamber will issue guidelines on the presentation of the Defence case and the filing of the schedule of witnesses will be dealt with. We envision the following: That the party calling the witness should file the list of witnesses for a month and this schedule should be filed 15 days before the first day of the relevant month. As for Mr. Prlic, his witnesses, the witnesses who will come and testify in May 2008, the Prlic Defence should file the list of witnesses who will come and testify on the 28th of April, 2008, at the latest. Mr. Karnavas, on the 28th of April at the latest, you should send us the list of witnesses who will come and testify the following month. Another thing we discussed this morning is that we would like to have a rolling schedule. In other words, every week you should update the schedule. You should send us a new list. This would enable us to have a clear idea about the witnesses who will come and testify. We have to consider also in that respect that the Chamber will need to decide how long cross-examination will take, cross-examination conducted by other Defence teams. And because of that, because we need to do that, we need to have the list of witnesses. I'm going to allow you to think about this, and before we have the break let me move on to the main item on this agenda, parties' comments on how much time the Trial Chamber plans to allocate for the presentation of the Defence case. You will be given 10 minutes each to speak. That's a total of one hour for the six Defence teams. As things stand now, on the basis of your submissions, of your filings, on the basis of what the Chamber knows about this case that has been going on for about two years, on the basis of the names of the witnesses, on the basis of the exhibits you have notified us of, we plan to allocate 80 hours to the Prlic Defence, and 54 hours to the Stojic Defence, 50 hours to the Praljak Defence, 50 hours to the Petkovic Defence, 45 hours to the Coric Defence, 22 hours and a half to the Pusic Defence team. Let me add that we are talking here about time dedicated to the examination-in-chief and to the examination-in-chief alone. Here we are not taking into account the time that will be taken by the Prosecution for cross-examination or by the other Defence teams for cross-examination purposes. We are not taking into account time spent on Judges' questions, and we are not taking into account either time spent on various procedural matters, incidents, objections, and so on and so forth. Based on the maths we've done during the Prosecution case, we find that Judges' questions take up about 10 per cent of the time. Procedural matters, incidents, take up about 22 per cent of the time. That's a ballpark figure. And in this particular case if the Prosecution is granted the same amount of time as the examination-in-chief for cross-examination, we would have a total of 301 hours and 30 minutes for the examination-in-chief, 50 per cent of that time for cross-examination for the other Defence teams, and we should need, roughly speaking, about 1.000 hours. A thousands hours starting on the 5th of May, because 5th of May will be the day when the trial begins again with the first opening statements. This is, of course, a ballpark figure, as I said. After the break you will have 10 minutes each, 10 minutes for each Defence team, to comment. We will very a break, but before that Judge Trechsel wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I want to share with you a problem we identified during our discussions. It's a problem related to re-examination by other Defence teams, re-examination of a witness called by another Defence team. That's part of the examination-in-chief. An example: The Prlic team, when organising its time, will need to take into account that it will need some -- to set aside some time. Why? Because this time set aside will be needed to supplement the examination-in-chief of another Defence team. I have the floor, and I'm going to return to English to be as clear as possible. [In English] What we mean by turning calendar, a rotating calendar. Now, and I make a very abstract example, we have on the 15th of April the calendar for 1 to 13 May. Then the next calendar we receive the 15th of May, by the 15th of May we have only two weeks ahead that we -- no. Then we get a calendar for 1 to 30 June, and 15 June a calendar 1 to 31 July. So we are jumping. The alternative possible is that we get one calendar on the 15th of April for the 1st to 31st May. Then a week later the 22nd of April we get one for the 7th May to the 7th June. Only 1 to 7 June will be new, in fact, will be added. And on the 1st of May, a week later, we'll have a calendar that goes from 15 May to 15 June. One week added in the end. In my view this will not cause additional work because you will be preparing all the time, and it makes a more regular rhythm in provisions what's going to happen. Just to make clear what was the meaning of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. As a matter of fact, I do not want to take much of our time because we are going to have a break, but I would like to recall that at the very last conference of ours here I did mention the percentages which had been taken up by various questions, and I recalled that procedural matters took 22 per cent of all of our time. Now the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, mentioned here that we found about the same amount of time, let's say about 22 per cent as procedural questions. I have already explained in our Chamber, and I do repeat here, that I am very much -- I will do my best to reduce the time allotted to procedure without any prejudice, of course, to the equity of arms and to the good running of this -- of this conference, and of course later on as far as the presentation of the defence. But I would like to emphasise that we should do our best as possible to reduce the time which is really almost one-fourth of the -- all the time allotted to these sittings and to the Prlic Chamber. So I repeat again that within the very well-known framework of the pre-trial, I ask all the parties and all those present here to do our best to try to reduce the 20 per cent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a wish that is common to all Judges. We're unanimous in that. We want this 20 per cent, this percentage, to be reduced. Most of this time is due to objections. Please try to reduce the number of objections. We understand when a question is a leading question. Just stand up and say objection and then sit down again. No need to go into lengthy discussions or speeches, because if you do that, if you just say "Objection," then the other party will just rephrase the question. In other Trial Chambers objections are seen as -- are considered as the time of the party making the objection. So please try not to spend so much time on these procedural matters because we spend so much time on this so far. What's important here is the substance of this case. The judgement will not hinge on whether a question has been put in a leading manner or not. That's not what's going to be taken into account. And when -- and during re-examination, do not forget to say when you put your questions, "The Prosecution said this," "The answer was this." "I have this additional question to put to you." In doing so we avoid any objections saying, "The question was not put that way" and so on and so forth. This will all be dealt with in our guidelines. The ideal would be for this 20 per cent to go down to 0 per cent. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Registrar, could release move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to counsels for the Defence regarding the hearing schedules, the Trial Chamber decided that when we would be sitting on Thursday afternoons, which will be the case when we resume, we will stop at 6.30 p.m. on Thursdays. The half hour lost, if I can call it so, will be retrieved for hearings that will be held on July 18th. It will be a Friday. Monday July 21st in the morning, and we will also have two additional hearings in October in order to make sure that there's no prejudice. But just as we do in the Seselj case, the hearing will stop at 6.30 p.m. on Thursdays. Now, this being said, Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor. Ten minutes. Remember that there are six of you that want to take the floor and we only have one hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. With my apologies to counsel, Your Honour. I wanted to raise it -- I did want to clarify one point that was brought up at the end of last session but given the speech about procedural time I was reluctant to pick it up but I will now. Your Honour, I think there was some -- and if I understand in talking to some of my colleagues on the other side, I think there was some confusion or lack of information, perhaps or maybe not, about the timing for Defence opening statements because based on something that was said a few moments ago before the break I had the impression that there was some thinking now that all these various opening statements by Mr. Praljak, by Mr. Petkovic, by Mr. Coric, by Mr. Pusic would all be made on the 5th of May, and it's my understanding that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then it is indeed different that what had been discussed that they were going to be made at the beginning of each respective Defence case. Frankly I don't care except to know so we can plan for whether we're having a witness on the 5th of May or the witness won't come for several days after that allowing for all the opening statements. But indeed there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are two ways to envisage this and proceed. Either each Defence team starts on the May 5th, D2, D3, and so on, D2 for 45 minutes and no one takes the floor, and no one makes an opening statement, but if it's -- and then we have D1 moving with -- hearing the first witness. We have no opening statement and we hear the first witness for D1. Is that it? This is up to you. This is up to the Defence to decide how they want about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, I don't have a strong feeling -- except -- the one way or the other except to know, but it was my impression based on the conversations today that there would be no opening statements on the 5th of May and we would go right to the first witness. Number one. That's point one number one. And my second very brief point, Your Honour, and just for the record, and Chamber's raised its concerns before and I think -- well, the Chamber, I'll leave it at that. For the record the Prosecution would state its objections to Mr. Praljak having another opening statement. Under the Rules he's already made a statement. That time has been done. He's made that statement. Unless the Chamber would like to give the Prosecution another statement somewhere along the way so that all sides get another statement, then we would consider that if the Chamber would allow the Prosecution to make a statement, but Mr. Praljak's made his statement. We would object to a second statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now regarding Mr. Praljak, I believe that the Trial Chamber had decided a few months back that he could make this opening statement. We said this when we made a decision on the 92 bis. So I refer you to this decision made by the Trial Chamber in this respect. I don't have it here, but just refer yourself to it. I'm almost sure that that's what is stated in this decision. Now, this being said, on May 5th we will be hearing the first witness for the Prlic Defence team, but there are two ways to proceed that are possible, having the opening statements all at once by all. That would have allowed us to have a general perspective on the different cases. It is true that in the Rules of Procedure opening statements are to be given right before the Defence case is presented for each accused, so we will wait for D2 to have the first opening statement. Mr. Karnavas, you have 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me state first that I was a little taken aback when I saw that the Trial Chamber had reduced the hours that we had indicated, which was 128 hours without Dr. Prlic's testimony to 80 hours, and from looking at the decision, and I call it a decision because it looks like a decision has already been made but you wish to have submissions in any event, does not reflect that the 80 hours also include the testimony for Dr. Prlic. So I guess first we need some clarification. Was the 80 hours in the 54 hours or the 50 hours for the arrests? Was that calculation -- does that include the testimony for the accused? I see Judge Trechsel indicating so. Recognising that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Recognising that we are not in a perfect world but where an accused is looking at a lifetime in prison where he grows old and dies in prison, recognising the fact that no one put limitations on the Prosecution to limit the scope of the indictment even though there was a change in the rules that would allow the Trial Chamber to influence to some extent, to focus or to reduce the indictment, recognising that this is primarily a documentation case and this was something that was brought up by the Prosecution when they were facing their problems in trying to introduce all those documents and we came up with this creative method of -- of submitting documents with basically nothing other than spin by the parties, leaving it up to the Judges to then decide how to use the documents, if you look at what we are presenting the witnesses, for instance, let me just give you an example. We heard from Professor/Judge Ribicic, the gentleman who came from Slovenia publishing the book with the Cevapci and I mention that because it's a derogatory way -- his derogatory way of showing what his contempt for his southern neighbours, in my opinion. This gentleman here had never heard of who Boras was, who Akmadzic was, who Pelivan was. All of these were central figures, anyone who would have done an expertise on the constitutionality, of which as he was asked to do so, would not have focused on one presidential transcript but rather would have spoken with these gentlemen. But in his testimony, if you recall, he never even heard of them. These gentlemen were with Mr. Izetbegovic during the time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was imploding, and the question was what, if any, government existed and to what extent it was able and capable of doing in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what other municipalities or regions could do and fend for themselves in light of the -- the circumstances there. If you look at the breadth and the depth of the indictment where you have Tudjman, Susak, Bobetko and the others, how can one deal with that within an hour or two? You do need somebody like Mr. -- like the gentleman that we propose, our very first witness, who was one of the insiders. He was there. Look at the list. They're ministers. They're prime ministers. They're foreign ministers. They're ambassadors. These are not, you know, crime base witnesses where we have five witnesses to testify about the very same thing. Now, during the presentation of the Prosecution case, I had, to use Judge Prandler's term, complained about the lack of time that was being allocated to me for cross-examination. I was complaining -- actually, I was making my record because there were several important witnesses which we did not get to thoroughly cross-examine, yet representations were made from the Bench of which I'm now going to remind the Bench of, which was that I would have all the time in the world. That was the expression, all the time in the world, to put on my defence. I'm not asking for all the time in the world. I'm not asking for a perfect world. I'm asking for a fair world. I'm asking for a fair process, and 80 hours with Dr. Prlic testifying is not only fair -- it's not fair, it's shameful. There is no way that I can conduct any case that is worth anything in light of all the testimony that has come from the Prosecution witnesses, in light of all the documents with that amount of time. Now, I've gone back and I've redone my math and this is the best I can do under the best of circumstances with 25 years of experience doing this work. I'm not some neophyte. This is not my first case here or anywhere else. I have been doing this business a long, long time before tough Judges. I need a minimum of 101 hours, and that's without Dr. Prlic testifying. And I cannot imagine where a Trial Chamber would put a limitation on the right of an accused as to how much he could testify to, because when you say 80 hours including him, something has to give. Either we don't present critical evidence to rebut evidence that came in from the Prosecution, or what you're saying is that an accused may have the right to testify but it's a -- it's a qualified right. "We will dictate how much time he will have." We cannot cover the subject matter. You had, for instance, one gentleman coming here, Mr. Tomljanovich, who prepared a report. Look at the report. Look at the footnotes. Look at what he's citing. Who better than these gentlemen here that we have on our list to explain all those things? How can you possibly understand what was happening if you don't allow us the time. And part of the problem with this case is that we have so many documents that even if you introduce documents wholesale through this new, inventive new procedure that we have that is nowhere else applicable, even under those conditions you still need to go through certain documents, and going through a document takes time. We've had hundreds of pages of presidential transcripts coming in where the Prosecution is latching on to one word, one phrase, one paragraph, one particular presidential transcript like Ribicic did, although I don't see how that's a constitutional analysis. How can you possibly go over that material by simply introducing it and giving it your own spin? What I say is not evidence. What the Prosecution says is not evidence. That's why I'm not giving an opening statement, because it's not evidence. Summation has a different value. You need to hear from the witnesses, the witnesses who were present, who can explain, and I can't imagine why the Trial Chamber would not want that testimony. Now, we've taken our time in preparing this list. We've met over 500 witnesses. We've scaled it down, and we've done this in a very rational manner. And I don't see anywhere in the Statute that it says that an accused's rights depends on the number of hours that the Prosecution case puts on, because that's what we're doing. We're saying that we're going to decide your rights based on hours and minutes and the case that you get to put on. I've tried cases where I've put on no case, where the Prosecution put on an extensive case or vice versa. Where the Prosecution put on a limited case, a small case, and I put on a very large, substantial Defence case with success. Why? Because I'm entitled to do that. I'm entitled to rebut the evidence. That's what we want to do, rebut the evidence that came in. We intend to produce evidence and to have testimony that is relevant, and I'll repeat again I've done this about a dozen times, and I'll keep doing it until this case is over. When it comes to questioning witnesses, be it one side or the other, there are two basic rules. Is it relevant, and is it non-repetitive? Those are the two universal rules that should apply here as they apply all around the world. Not you've got your three minutes, hurry up. So I go back. We cannot do it in 80 hours. If we were forced to go with 80 hours and Dr. Prlic, I would be prepared to tell Dr. Prlic to simply sit in his cell and not come out. This is not fair. This would be a process that I could not agree to, and I could not advise my client to proceed. You've told us that you will give us all the time in the world. Those were your words. We're not asking for all the time. We're asking for fair time, and I'm entitled to that fair time because Dr. Prlic is entitled to that fair time. And I don't know how the 80 hours -- how this Trial Chamber came up with the 80 hours. I certainly would want to know for the purposes of the record. If the Trial Chamber insists on 80 hours, including Dr. Prlic, I would like an explanation, a detailed explanation as to how the Bench came up with that amount of hours, because I can -- I've given my breakdown. You've seen my documents that go to every witness. You see where they go to every paragraph. I want an explanation from the Bench for the record so we can appeal before we start, but I cannot truncate my case any more than it has been. It is what it is based on the indictment. I cannot control what the Prosecution's indictment is going to be or the documents they intend to produce. That is their case. They're entitled to their case. We've fought long and we've fought hard with them to have their right to put on their case based on their -- their analysis. They wanted 400 hours. We said give them 400. You cut it to 300. You gave them some more time. Not as much as they wanted but nonetheless we thought back then it was a mistake because they know their case. This is an adversarial setting. There is to dossier in this case. So we say based on what you've heard, based on what you've heard, based on the documentation that you have before you, based on the documentation that we have shown you that we intend to present through our witnesses, some of which can come through motion, but most of it need to come through the witness so they -- you can hear, so we can make a record, because I dare say records are necessary for appeals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, we have heard you and duly noted what you said. The Trial Chamber spent almost two months thinking about this independently of the request for provisional freedom that also took a lot of our time. We have been working on this for two months extensively, starting with your witness list. For your first list you were asking for 66 hours and for your list number two 62 hours, and we assessed every -- each and every witness, and in the framework of this -- of what we've done, reducing time for witnesses -- let me give you an example. The London conference, for example. Witness number 8 on your list, I don't know if you've asked protective measures but I will not give his name. You had planned for eight hours. The London conference we've spent hours talking about it, hours and hours and hours, and you needed another eight hours? We believed and estimated that four hours was plenty. So altogether with 80 hours, we're talking about your witnesses for about 300 hours. 80 hours for you, 80 hours for Prosecution, 40 hours for cross-examination, questions from the Bench, procedural incidents, and so on. Altogether we've spent 300 hours we estimated, 50 hours for the witnesses, 30 hours for your client. And your client will testify. You can go back on the London conference on Greater Croatia, on the visas granted to refugees, on the ABiH and so forth and so on. In my own jurisdiction, let me tell you in my own jurisdiction five or six hours would have been enough to complete all this, and you have 20 times, 30 times more time. What do you want? What can I say? That's the first thing. Second thing, Prosecution had 300 hours altogether, and this was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. So Defence has 300 hours. That gives us two years altogether. We're in this Tribunal for two more years. So giving you 120 hours, fine. Two hundred hours while we're at it, but we'd need eternity in this Tribunal and unfortunately we don't have eternal in front of us so we have to stop things at one point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I propose that we do not carry out now a discussion. The President has allocated ten minutes to each of the teams and it's already only 40 minutes. In some way you will get an answer for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want an answer without a record because I'm entitled to reply because the gentleman that he has singled out is perhaps one of the most -- it's not just about that conference. He's been -- in the entire period of the indictment he's involved in these issues. His name has popped up. There are all sorts of exhibits. That's number one. And number two as far as the French system you have an investigative judge and you have a dossier. We don't have that here. There lies the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry. If you want to discuss every witness we are here for the rest of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wanted to rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wanted to reply. I wanted to reply because one is singled out, and you say, Well, the London conference. It's not just about the London conference. It's about four years of the indictment, and I've heard repeatedly from even you, Judge Trechsel, that I would have sufficient time. You're not giving me sufficient time. That's the problem that I'm having. That's why I'm getting excited. That's why I think must go to my client and say, "Stay in your cell, boycott this procedure." This is not fair. Eighty hours is not fair no matter how you slight it and dice it. We all want to go home but we want a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's hear now from D2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to repeat some of the things my colleague has already said, but I must say that we fully agree with his position that we had estimated our time in a highly restrictive manner. I must say on behalf of Mr. Stojic's Defence that our estimates were restrictive. They were below the minimum. Bearing in mind throughout this problem of time constraint, this pressure, in my view, I will say this for the first and only time perhaps, has reached an absurd level when my distinguished Judge Prandler says that I will refrain from procedural objections. For us procedural objections by the learned Judges are of the greatest importance. These objections contribute to the quality of this trial. If we go so far as to refrain from objecting, then the only factor is time, and if time is the only factor, then we cannot have a fair trial. Mr. Stojic's Defence asked for 68 hours. Their Honours had occasion to see that we envisaged a certain number of witnesses, that even though there are several of them who will be speaking about similar issues, they will not comment on the same facts. We were highly restrictive bearing in mind this pressure of time, and we envisaged a minimum, a necessary minimum. I am additionally disturbed today if out of the 54 hours proposed by the Trial Chamber I have to reserve for myself 10 hours for the examination of other witnesses who might confirm some of my thesis in the Defence case, then I must radically change the minimum amount of time I have requested. I wish to appeal to the Trial Chamber to reconsider their decision bearing in mind only one additional fact, and that is that the Prosecution through their submissions tendered one-third of the exhibits. That is their right. We will have the same right. The Prosecutor did so because they were also suffering under the pressure of time, but the Defence has the additional pressure of all the witnesses that will be coming here to rebut those exhibits. Almost a third of those exhibits need to be challenged through our witnesses. Your Honours, you have seen the list of witnesses for Mr. Stojic, and you have seen the exhibits that will be produced through those witnesses, but we were not obliged to put on the 65 ter list the exhibits that we will be showing the witnesses. You have seen how the witnesses are structured. They are mostly witnesses who worked in the defence department, and through each of those witnesses we will be checking out certain allegations that are already in the exhibits that have been admitted. The very number of documents given is not sufficient to judge where -- how much time is needed. Therefore, I appeal to Your Honours to reconsider once again, especially as we need to reserve time for the witnesses of other Defence teams, because I think that we were highly -- very fair in our estimates of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D3. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to make a statement because actually Ms. Nozica has referred to my statement as a kind of antonym argument. So therefore I have to underline the following: She said that I was saying in line 17, page 87, that I asked you to refrain, that you should refrain from procedural objections, and it was actually written there in the transcript. So I would like to say that I have not said this, and I have not talked about this kind of refraining from procedural objections. What I was saying, referring to the fact that during these last two years we have used 22 per cent of our time for procedural questions, that we have to do something just to leave more time to you, to the Defence, to do its business, and if we are taking away 22 per cent for procedural questions of the whole time, then of course less time is going to be given to the Defence and to all of us. So it has been my point, and therefore I would like to repeat that I have never said this. On the contrary. I did refer to Article 20 of the Statute of ours, and of course we recall that paragraph 1 of Article 20 speaks about it, what I did refer to, that the Trial Chambers shall ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, et cetera, and I -- again why I wanted to refer to this Article of the Statute is that definitely this Chamber, myself, and all my fellow Judges are for this Rule, and therefore I wouldn't like to -- to be -- you to misread my own position on that matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one sentence. Quotation marks are missing from the transcript. I didn't say that Your Honour said that we must refrain from procedural objections. I said that he said that he would refrain from procedural objections, and I expressed regret because I think every procedural issue discussed by the Chamber, whether it comes from the Chamber or the parties, can certainly contribute to the quality of the proceedings. I'm afraid that the interpretation was wrong. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will continue this time on English because I have prepared paper and because of terminology it would be probably easier or more correct. I will not go too much into the law. We all know the basic guarantees of the Statute and as well as appropriate norms of -- of the Rules. However, when it comes to the law, I would like to refer to Appeals Chamber in Oric. This is a decision on length of Defence case from 20 July 2005, where some standards were established. First, the Appeals Chamber says: "Equality of arms obligates a judicial body to ensure that neither party is put at disadvantage when presenting its case. The Trial Chamber's order limiting the accused in this case to approximately 27 days of direct testimony after 100 days used by the Prosecution. The Appeals Chamber held that the disparity in this instance is so great that no specific prejudice need to be shown in order for them to overturn the decision by the Trial Chamber." And this is the law, and I think this is established law on this court. What is Praljak Defence strategy? What is our goal, and what is our task? What we should do in the Defence case? It could be put very simply. First, we must respond to Prosecution approach of selective use of facts and evidence. Second, and this is specific Defence goal, a complete -- we must provide a complete picture regarding defendant which, if nothing else, means actus reus and mens rea, of course reflecting all specific events or accounts. To use a metaphor which my distinguished colleague invented, I should say, the Prosecution's approach has been to take a penlight into a dark room and illuminate a few aspects of what lies in the room, and with those carefully selected aspects tell a story of a vast conspiracy which implicates my client. Our strategy, Defence strategy, is not to pick over those same items but to light the room as best we can, to provide the complete picture surrounding my client which contradicts in holistic and comprehensive sense the supposed vast conspiracy connected to my client which the Prosecution alleges is implied by the evidence it has selectively put forward. And this is our strategy, and this is our assignment. A couple of words on the issue of law as applied to the facts, or in other words, opportunity to present Praljak Defence. Proposed reduction of time, by "proposed" I mean on intentions you put on paper, would violate the principle of the equality of arms and lead to miscarriage of justice. The amount of time allocated to Praljak Defence is not reasonably proportional to the fair opportunity to present this case. Next, the Appeals Chamber in Oric held that: "Although Rule 73 ter gives the Trial Chamber the authority to limit the length of time and number of witnesses allocated to the Defence case, such restrictions are always subject to the general requirement that the rights of the accused pursuant to Article 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal be respected." And third, Your Honours intend to allow us a mere 17 per cent of the time the Prosecution used in its case. We know from the Appeals Chamber that 27 per cent in a much simpler case, which was in Oric, was considered so disproportionate that the Appeals Chamber dismissed it out of hand. The fact that there are other accused in this case does not suffice to bridge the enormous gap between the Prosecution's time and the time proposed for the Praljak Defence. The reasons are the following: Having co-accused is not a condition most accused wish for. We didn't choose it; the Prosecution did. Next, procedural position is -- procedural position of an accused and his right to defence guaranteed by the Statute must not be limited regardless of the number of co-accused in the case. In multi-accused case, each of the accused must have the same rights as they would have if they were accused alone. And the last point on this issue, Your Honours may rule that certain items are duplicative of evidence already presented and thus shorten our time, but that must be done on a case-by-case basis, not a priori by limitation of time to present evidence in defence. Being aware of time constraints in preparing a scope of Defence evidence, i.e., Rule 65 ter (G) lists, Praljak Defence was extremely selective, and I'm referring your attention to paragraph 5 of our 31st March submission where we explain our position. We have been planning to use Rule 92 ter -- bis -- or bis mechanism very extensively in order to contribute to the efficiency of the trial. This is clearly demonstrated by the fact that only 22 witnesses in such a big indictment have been planned as viva voce witnesses, 38 witnesses as 92 ter and quater witnesses, and 156 witnesses as 92 bis witnesses. This shows something. This simply -- the Trial Chamber intends to allocate to Praljak only 52 per cent of the time requested by Rule 65 ter submission. This simply cannot be done by abandoning some crucial evidence. This is close to mission impossible. This would result in a clear and substantial breach of the defendant's rights guaranteed by the Tribunal Statute and jurisprudence. In conclusion, Praljak Defence requests a total of 97 hours for presentation of the Defence case depending on the realisation of the plans of other co-accused. Praljak defence will do whatever is necessary in order to avoid repetitive or irrelevant evidence, and that is my submission, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me first of all to compare the times planned here for particular Defence teams with the time that was given to the Prosecution. All the Defence teams together should be allocated to 301 and a half hours. At the same time, the Prosecutor had a relatively more significant amount of time. At this moment it is really not relevant whether the Prosecution has used the time or not. We believe that this ratio between the time given to the Prosecution and the six Defence teams together is not fair and that it constitutes the breach of the rights of the accused to defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, one correction. The exact time for the -- allocated to the Prosecution was 217 hours. 297, correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Trial Chamber had reduced the time that the Prosecution had requested and the Appeals Chamber confirmed to us this reduction of time, and then the Prosecution had requested additional -- an additional time of 27 hours or something to that effect which was granted to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so, Your Honours. And when you add up all the times, the Prosecution had at its disposal 319 hours, and the fact is that the Prosecution has not used all those hours as a matter of certain circumstances or a conscious decision on the part of the Prosecution. If the Prosecution's time is compared with the times planned for the Defence teams and in this particular moment I'm only interested in the time allocated for general Petkovic's defence, we can see that this allocation of time would not have been allocated to General Petkovic if he was the only accused before the Trial Chamber, which constitutes a breach of Rule 82 of the rules of evidence which says that the accused in joint trials have the same rights and enjoy the same rights as in the case of single accused. This does not allow for a fair trial either for the General Petkovic or his co-accused. And within that context I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of your own words, and I would like to paraphrase not in the same way as my learned friend Karnavas did. In the Prosecution case the Defence teams often complained about the times that was given to them for cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. We always complained about a lack of time to challenge the Prosecutor's allegations, and we also complained that we did not have the time to try and analyse or comment the evidence presented to us by the Prosecution through certain witnesses. In explaining the allocated time, the Trial Chamber as a rule would tell us you would have enough time during your cases to challenge all what the Prosecution has alleged and also comment upon the documents that have been presented by the Prosecution. I would like to point out at this moment that when allocating times to certain Defence teams it doesn't really matter only how many witnesses have been envisaged by a certain Defence team and how much evidence, but it is also important to allow the Defence times to the extent they deem relevant to challenge the Prosecution case and present to the Trial Chamber in a different way the documents that have already been admitted into evidence as tendered by the Prosecution. Further on, if we analyse the Prosecution case, we will see that most of the Prosecution witnesses as a rule were those that through which documentary evidence was presented to the Trial Chamber, and this evidence was then admitted into evidence. This will certainly be expected from the Defence teams, and as may be seen from our list, the Defence teams have prepared their -- their cases in a similar way. That's why when calculating the time one should bear in mind how many documents that are relevant for the case will be tendered into evidence by the Defence teams. And it is very easy to make a calculation as to how much within the 50 hours allocated time could be presented to the Trial Chamber without hearing the witnesses. I'm talking about 300 documents, which is approximately one-tenth or one-twentieth of the documents that particular Defence teams have planned to present in this courtroom. If a Defence team is to be allowed to tender documents in the same way the Prosecution did, then the Defence team should be allowed more time than has been envisaged in the draft decision of the Honourable Chamber. Moreover, the Defence teams should be allowed to bring witnesses that will support the Defence case to explain not only where the accused were, what they did, what their knowledge and intentions were, but also they have would to have an opportunity to explain about the body where the accused work, how that body worked, and as General Praljak would put it, they would also have to be able to present the situation on the ground, the abilities or impossibilities to work in one way or another as would normally be expected in a society where there are established rules of behaviour and where there is a highly developed democracy. Faced with the social changes that were taking place in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of the 1990s, and now I'm going to say something that is not disputed in the sociology of war, such social changes and destruction of the former political social systems takes place that it takes years upon years to establish new rules of the game. We're trying individuals for acting or not acting in a certain way and for events in which they did not have a role to play in the moments of such a social breakdown when there were no judicial or any other social bodies which could be expected to act in a way they would normally do in developed democracies and stable systems. In order to explain all that to the Trial Chamber, we really do need a relatively more time than has been planned in draft decision. The Defence for General Petkovic has tried to reduce both the number of witnesses and the times allocated to them and I believe that our requests should be adopted because the witnesses that we propose and the topics that they will talk about go to all the counts in the indictment that all concern the military and military commanders. Believe -- we believe that these topics are of significance for all the accused, and we want to demonstrate that by -- that when creating the HVO army and conducting certain combat activities there was no criminal intent or a joint criminal enterprise that our accused are charged with in the indictment. That's why we're asking the Trial Chamber to consider the possibility to take into consideration our proposal for the maximum of allocated time, and if not, then we hope that any decision will be explained in a sufficient measure to allow us to understand all the restrictions so that if we deem that there is grounds for appeal that we should be able to appeal any such decision. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... for Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I we will not repeat what we heard from my predecessors said. I can only say that I agree with all of them and join them in their motions. As far as the Coric Defence is concerned I would like to say the following. When we were putting together our lists, we tried to reduce the number of witnesses and the time needed to hear them in the courtroom and we have tried to rationalise this in the best possible way and to reduce the time to a minimum. A majority of our witnesses is not a majority but all of them are viva voce witnesses. They are viva voce not because we did not want them to be 92 ter or 92 bis witnesses but because all these witnesses held such positions and possessed such knowledge which entitles them to testify not only about the documents that we have on our 65 ter list but also about those documents that have already been admitted into evidence in -- during the Prosecution case. That is why we have very little room for manoeuvre and very little space to adapt to such a curtailed time. The only way for us to hear these witnesses or to deal with these witnesses is to give up on a number of them, and we, just like my learned friend Karnavas had talked to a much larger number of people than are on my list now, so we have already reduced our numbers and we can't go any further than that, or alternatively we could hear some of them as 92 ter witnesses instead of viva voce but this creates a problem. If we introduce a witness as a 92 ter witness then the number of documents that we can hear with the witness is limited, and we can certainly not comment upon all those documents that have already been admitted into evidence if we opt for these witnesses to be 92 ter. This much from the Coric Defence. I would only kindly ask you to take all our arguments together with the arguments that were presented so far into consideration. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We asked for 22 and a half hours for Mr. Pusic's Defence and the Trial Chamber agreed with that and we're satisfied that our interests at this moment are well-served and we have no objections to the time allocated to us for the Pusic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to set the time. We've taken note of what you've said. Mr. Scott is going to give us his pointed of view as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm happy that the Chamber was going to allow the Prosecution some time to be heard on this issue. Your Honour, very briefly. Everyone in this courtroom knows that time has been an issue in this case for a very, very long time, and it was the Prosecution case -- Prosecution which has the burden of proof, the Prosecution which has the obligation to the victims of this case, to the international community, and to the professional carrying out of its functions, to present its case in a professional way and with those heavy obligations in mind. Having said that, the Chamber cut the Prosecution case substantially. We had originally asked the Chamber for 450 hours, 450 hours. It was then initially cut to 290 -- 293 hours, which was about 65 per cent of the time we had asked for. Then we asked for some additional time toward the end of our case, and although the Chamber granted it, we actually wound up using 296 hours and 25 minutes. We'll call that 297 hours. My very good friend Ms. Alaburic is not correct when she says that we simply made a decision that Prosecution didn't use all the time allowed and not using the entire 23 hours. What the record will plainly show is that the Chamber in addition to the hours allocated also set a date certain for the determination of the Prosecution case on the 24th of January, 2008, and I'm sure that everyone in the courtroom will recall that I very carefully and very deliberately did not rest the Prosecution case. I did not say the Prosecution had no other evidence to present. I did not say we had completed the Prosecution case. The time expired. The Chamber had a stopwatch set for the 24th of January, 2008. We reached 2008. The Prosecution sat down, walked out. The door was closed. That was the end of the Prosecution case. We did not rest but that was the time that the Chamber had given us. I also refer to the Oric case, the decision that's been used and the decision of the Appeals Chamber from the 20th of July, 2005. This particular pertinent language has not been referenced just yet. On page 6, paragraph 7 of the Appeals Chamber's decision written and signed by

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: "At a minimum equality of arms obligates a judicial body to ensure that neither party," I emphasise the word "neither," that includes the Prosecution, "that neither party is put at a disadvantage when presenting its case, certainly in terms of procedural equity. This is not to say, however, that an accused is necessarily entitled to precisely the same amount of time or the same number of witnesses as the Prosecution. The Prosecution has the burden of telling an entire story or putting together a coherent narrative and proving every necessary element of the crimes charged beyond a reasonable doubt. Defence strategy by contrast," and this is not Ken Scott speaking, I'm quoting the Appeals Chamber, "Defence strategy by contrast often focuses on poking specifically targeted holes in the Prosecution case, an endeavour which may require less time and fewer witnesses. This is sufficient reason to explain why a principle of basic proportionality rather than a strict principle of mathematical equality generally governs the relationship between the time and witnesses allocated to the two sides." The Prosecution, Your Honour, is never going to argue that if you give a few additional hours to the Defence we got 293, they get 302, they get 310, Prosecution is never going to argue about such a few additional hours, but, and I have -- given the history of this case, I have to make it very clear if the -- if the Chamber were to give the Defence substantially greater time than it gave to the Prosecution in this case, it would be a fundamental miscarriage of justice. It would not be fair to the victims in the case -- in this case. It would not be fair to the Prosecution. It would not be fair to international community and serious question would have to be given if the trial could go forward under such a cloud of such unfairness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 7.00 p.m. The Judges will review today's transcript. We'll issue a decision very shortly. The parties will be in a position to view our decision. That's all I have to say. Of course we ask the D1 team to send us their witness list very shortly because we'll be starting on the 5th of May, in two weeks. Have a pleasant evening, and we'll meet again on the 5th of May.
